content: When individuals present for HIV testing, healthcare providers may not always be able to determine whether the person is already aware of their HIV status or if they were previously engaged in care but have since transferred to another facility or been lost to follow-up (LTFU). For these individuals, ensuring linkage from HIV testing services (HTS) to antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation or re-initiation is critical. Disaggregated reporting of this indicator by time since diagnosis (e.g., within 28 or 90 days) and timing of ART initiation provides insights into the quality of care and adherence to national guidelines, including rapid ART initiation within seven days of diagnosis. Programs can also analyze linkage to ART for individuals diagnosed in the past six months by selecting the appropriate time period in the disaggregation. Coupled with ART coverage data, this indicator helps programs assess their ability to connect diagnosed individuals to treatment and care services. Partner services, also known as provider-assisted referral, are an effective strategy to identify additional people living with HIV. Partners of diagnosed individuals who test positive can be linked to treatment services, while those who test negative can be connected to prevention services. In this approach, providers contact partners via phone, email, or in person to offer HTS. Partner notification and testing must be voluntary and supported by appropriate services, with the consent of the index partner and strict confidentiality of data. The service cascade can be evaluated by tracking the percentage of partners accepting services and the number of partners tested, accounting for those already aware of their HIV-positive status. Community-based HIV testing services (HTS), including HIV self-testing (HIVST), are expanding access to testing among hard-to-reach, high-risk populations. These services can be delivered in various settings, such as fixed community locations, mobile vans, homes, workplaces, and places of worship. Community-based HTS often involve trained lay providers or peers using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Data from these services complement facility-based testing and improve linkage to care. Community-based venues may focus on key populations, providing critical data for follow-up and targeted service delivery. The 2020 HIV strategic information guidelines recommend tracking HIVST kit distribution in both community and facility settings for prevention and treatment linkage. Reactive HIVST results should always be followed by confirmatory testing by a trained provider. However, many HIVST models face challenges in tracking progression from kit distribution to confirmatory testing and linkage to care. Depending on the context, data collection at the facility level may include testing registers or dedicated HIVST distribution registers to record kit distribution, population groups receiving kits, and prior HIVST use. Additional data fields may track confirmatory testing and linkage to care, balancing feasibility and provider workload. HIV testing services for key populations are essential for prevention, early diagnosis, and linkage to care. These services should be routinely offered in both community and facility-based settings. Data confidentiality and security are critical, particularly when sharing sensitive information such as HIV status or stigmatized behaviors. Anonymous unique identifiers (UIDs) are recommended instead of national identity numbers to protect client confidentiality. Robust systems for data security enable community service providers to collect and use sensitive data effectively, supporting integrated service delivery. Monitoring ART initiation and clinical management should follow person-centered care principles, focusing on the health needs and preferences of individuals and communities. Rapid ART initiation, recommended by WHO since 2017, involves starting ART within seven days of diagnosis, preferably on the same day, for individuals ready to begin treatment. Patient monitoring tools and electronic medical record (EMR) systems should be updated to track rapid treatment initiation. ART initiation timing varies based on clinical conditions, such as tuberculosis (TB) or cryptococcal meningitis, with specific recommendations for each scenario. For example, ART should be delayed by 4–6 weeks in cases of cryptococcal meningitis to reduce mortality risk. Late ART initiation often reflects treatment interruptions, disengagement from care, or challenges in linkage to services. Among children, late diagnosis is associated with missed opportunities for early testing and delays in the infant diagnosis cascade. Social factors, such as caregiver availability and readiness, also contribute to delays in ART initiation for children. Monitoring postnatal attendance, early infant diagnosis (EID) coverage, and age at ART initiation can help address these issues. Additionally, tracking turnaround times for test results and time from diagnosis to ART initiation is essential. Monitoring treatment outcomes, including viral suppression, is critical for assessing program success. Viral load (VL) testing should occur at six and 12 months after ART initiation and annually thereafter. Patient monitoring systems should capture early VL testing to promote adherence and suppression. Updated WHO recommendations emphasize the importance of routine VL monitoring and CD4 count testing, particularly for advanced HIV disease or re-engagement in care. ART toxicity monitoring has also been revised to include emerging issues such as weight gain and cardiometabolic toxicities. Patient monitoring tools should be updated to reflect these changes and support comprehensive care for people living with HIV.
